timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: What's Active Directory? I hear about it at work all the time.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Active Directory is the central nervous system of enterprise IT. It manages every user account, every computer, every policy. When you log into your work laptop, AD decides if you're allowed in.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: So it's like the boss of the network?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: More like the king. And attackers know that if they compromise the king, they own the kingdom. 95% of enterprise breaches involve AD compromise.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: The most common attack is Kerberoasting. Attackers request service tickets for service accounts, then crack them offline. Service accounts often have weak passwords.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: Can't you just make strong passwords?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: You should, but many organizations have hundreds of service accounts with passwords that haven't been changed in years. Some are even in Group Policy Preferences with encrypted passwords that are trivially decryptable.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Golden Ticket attacks are even worse. If an attacker gets the KRBTGT hash, they can create authentication tickets for ANY account. Total domain compromise.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: How do you defend against that?

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Regular KRBTGT password rotations, monitoring for anomalous Kerberos activity, implementing tiered admin accounts, and using tools like BloodHound to map attack paths before attackers do.

timeline.speaker: Stewie
timeline.text: Interview tip: explain the Kerberos authentication flow, common AD attacks, and defense strategies. This is guaranteed to come up in any pentest or SOC interview.

timeline.speaker: Peter
timeline.text: I had no idea AD was this critical and this vulnerable.
